A Third Party Logistics Provider, often abbreviated as 3PL, refers to a company or service provider that offers outsourced logistics and supply chain management services to businesses. A 3PL acts as an intermediary between manufacturers, retailers, and customers, facilitating the movement and storage of goods from one point to another.The primary role of a 3PL is to handle various logistics functions on behalf of their clients. These functions may include transportation, warehousing, inventory management, order fulfillment, packaging, customs brokerage, and freight forwarding. The specific services provided by a 3PL can vary depending on the needs of the client and the capabilities of the provider.By outsourcing logistics activities to a 3PL, businesses can focus on their core competencies while relying on the expertise and infrastructure of the service provider to streamline their supply chain operations. This can lead to improved efficiency, reduced costs, and enhanced customer satisfaction. 3PLs often leverage advanced technologies and industry expertise to optimize processes and provide value-added services.Overall, a Third Party Logistics Provider plays a crucial role in managing the logistics and supply chain activities of businesses, allowing them to operate more effectively in the increasingly complex and globalized marketplace.

Intermodal shipment refers to the transportation of goods using multiple modes of transportation, such as rail, road, water, and air. Intermodal shipments offer several advantages, and there are several attributes associated with this mode of transportation. Here are some common attributes of intermodal shipments:Multiple Modes: Intermodal shipments involve the use of multiple modes of transportation, allowing for seamless movement of goods across different networks. It can include combinations of trucks, trains, ships, and planes.Efficiency: Intermodal transportation is often more efficient than using a single mode of transportation. Each mode is utilized for its strengths, such as rail for long distances, trucks for last-mile delivery, and ships for overseas transport. This results in cost savings, reduced transit times, and improved supply chain performance.Flexibility: Intermodal shipments provide flexibility in choosing the most suitable transportation modes and routes based on factors like cost, time, and geographical considerations. It allows for better adaptation to changing market conditions and enables businesses to optimize their logistics operations.Interconnectivity: Intermodal transportation involves the interconnectivity of different modes, enabling the seamless transfer of goods from one mode to another. This is achieved through well-coordinated logistics hubs, terminals, and specialized containers or trailers that can be easily transferred between modes.Containerization: Containers play a crucial role in intermodal shipments. Standardized shipping containers enable efficient handling, loading, and unloading of goods across different modes of transportation. They provide protection to the cargo, simplify logistics operations, and enhance security during transit.Tracking and Visibility: Intermodal shipments often incorporate advanced tracking and visibility technologies, such as GPS and RFID (Radio Frequency Identification), to monitor the location and status of goods throughout the transportation process. This enhances supply chain visibility, improves security, and enables better management of inventory and customer expectations.Environmental Benefits: Intermodal transportation can offer environmental benefits by reducing fuel consumption and emissions. The use of rail or water transport for long-haul segments can be more energy-efficient and emit fewer greenhouse gases compared to relying solely on trucks for transportation.Cost Savings: Intermodal shipments can help reduce transportation costs by leveraging the advantages of different modes. By selecting the most cost-effective modes for different segments of the journey, businesses can optimize their transportation spend and improve overall profitability.These attributes highlight the advantages of intermodal shipments and why they are favored by many businesses for their transportation needs.

Creating secure authentication workflows can be a tricky business, but it's great that you're giving this a lot of thought. Here are some options you might consider:Use a dynamic, non-secret value as a salt: Instead of hard-coding the salt or including it in the link, you could derive it from some other value that you're already sending. For example, you could use a hashed version of the user's email as the salt. This would provide unique salts for each user without you having to store them anywhere. However, since the email address itself isn't secret, this wouldn't necessarily add a lot of security - it would primarily serve to thwart precomputed dictionary attacks ("rainbow tables").Include the salt in the link: While you're right that this reduces security somewhat, it might be a reasonable compromise given your requirements. A potential attacker would still need to break your encryption in order to use the link, and if your encryption is strong, this should be difficult. To make the links safer, consider using a secure random generator to produce the salt.Store the salt in a user session: This could work, but user sessions typically live on the server, so this would contradict your requirement of not touching the database (unless you're using a stateless JWT-style session, in which case you're back to sending the salt to the client).JWT tokens: You could use JSON Web Tokens (JWT) to create the magic links. JWTs are a compact, URL-safe means of representing claims to be transferred between two parties. You can include the user's email and an expiration time in the token, then sign it using a secret key. When the user clicks the link, you validate the token and, if it's valid and not expired, the email is verified. You don't need to store anything in the database, and there's no need for a salt because you're not hashing anything. The downside is that if an attacker gets your secret key, they can create valid tokens.TOTP for random numbers: If you're asking users to enter random numbers, consider using Time-based One-Time Password (TOTP) algorithm. It generates a one-time password based on the current time and a secret key. The server knows the secret key and can generate its own OTPs to compare with what the user entered. The nice thing about TOTP is that it automatically includes expiration (because the OTP changes over time), and if you only accept each OTP once, it can't be reused even if it's intercepted.In general, make sure to use secure, up-to-date cryptographic algorithms and libraries. Older algorithms and libraries may have known vulnerabilities that make your system easier to attack. Consider also rate limiting attempts to use the magic link to mitigate brute force attacks.

Option 1: This is a simple and effective approach for thwarting precomputed dictionary attacks, but keep in mind it is only as secure as the hash function you use. Since the salt isn't secret, a potential attacker could still make an offline attack if they get hold of your hashed data and know your algorithm. However, if you're using a strong encryption algorithm and a sufficiently complex key, this should be difficult.Option 2: There's not much difference in terms of security between options 1 and 2, but option 2 may be a bit simpler to implement. The main consideration here is that the salt should be randomly generated and sufficiently long to make guessing it impractical. Also, you should make sure that the generated links are only valid for a limited period of time to prevent their reuse if they are intercepted or leaked.Option 3: Putting the salt in a cookie would mean that it is tied to a specific browser, which could be inconvenient for users as you've noted. The risk of someone hacking into people's emails varies depending on the sensitivity of the data your app is handling. For most consumer applications, it's probably not a high risk, but it's not nonexistent either. If you're dealing with highly sensitive data, you might want to consider a more secure approach.Option 4: JWT tokens are signed but not encrypted by default, meaning the payload data can be read by anyone who intercepts the token. If an attacker has the secret key, they can forge tokens, which would be a problem. The key here is to keep the secret key secure. As for rainbow table attacks, they're more applicable to hashed values (like password hashes), not signed tokens like JWT. As long as you use a strong, secure secret key, rainbow attacks aren't really a concern for JWTs.Option 5: TOTP is a good solution, especially because it naturally prevents reuse of the code. However, typical TOTP codes are 6 digits long, which might be a bit long for users to type without errors. It could work in the query param for a magic link, but again, you would need to ensure that the magic link is used within a limited time frame. In practice, many services send TOTP codes via SMS or through an authenticator app. Remember, TOTP requires a shared secret between the server and the client. This secret must be securely stored and kept confidential, which might present its own challenges.Remember, security is all about trade-offs. Consider the sensitivity of the data you're protecting and the risks associated with different methods, and choose the method that provides an appropriate level of security for your specific situation.

Implementing TOTP (Time-based One-Time Password) from scratch without using existing libraries is possible, but it's a non-trivial task. The TOTP algorithm is defined in RFC 6238, and involves a number of cryptographic operations, including HMAC-SHA1 hashing and Base32 encoding.Here's a rough outline of the steps you would need to follow:Generate a Secret Key: This will be a random binary string, typically 80 bits or longer. You could generate it using a cryptographically secure random number generator.Share the Secret Key: You need to securely share this secret key with the user. Often this is done by creating a QR code that the user can scan using an authenticator app.Generate the TOTP: This involves several steps:Calculate the number of time steps between an epoch (usually 1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC) and the current time. The time step is typically 30 seconds.Convert this time step value to a byte array.Calculate the HMAC-SHA1 hash of this byte array, using the secret key.Perform some operations on this hash to convert it into a 6-digit number.Validate the TOTP: When the user provides a TOTP, you need to repeat the generation process and see if you get the same result.There are a number of complexities here, including handling time synchronization issues, ensuring all your cryptographic operations are secure, and dealing with different encodings and data types. Implementing these yourself can be error-prone and is generally not recommended unless you have a very good reason for doing so.If you're concerned about dependencies, one option could be to use a smaller, more focused library that only handles the HMAC-SHA1 and Base32 encoding parts, and implement the TOTP-specific parts yourself. But in general, using a well-maintained and widely-used library like speakeasy is going to be both safer and easier.

Using the same secret key for all users could pose a security risk. Here's why:The secret key is essentially the seed for the one-time password generation. If you're using the same secret key for all users, then the OTP generated at any given time will be the same for all users. This means that if an attacker manages to intercept or otherwise acquire a valid OTP, they could potentially use it to impersonate any user.Additionally, if the shared secret key were to be compromised (e.g., if an attacker gained access to your environment variables), they would be able to generate valid OTPs for any user. In contrast, if each user has a unique secret key, an attacker who compromises one key would only be able to impersonate that one user.That said, there may be scenarios where a shared key might be acceptable, depending on the specifics of your application and threat model. For example, if you're generating OTPs that are only used once and then immediately expired, and you have other layers of security in place, it might be less of a risk.However, it's generally considered best practice to use unique keys for each user to minimize the potential impact of a key being compromised.If you're looking to avoid creating a database table, one possibility might be to derive a unique secret key for each user based on some other unique attribute of the user (like their user ID or email), combined with a master key stored as an environment variable. But this has its own potential issues (for instance, you would need to handle key derivation securely), and in general it's still advisable to store per-user secret keys in a secure manner, which typically means a dedicated database table.

Given that you're open to using a database and want to maintain both the magic link and short code verification options, here's a proposed solution:Create a Database Table: You will need a table to store the secret keys for each user, along with the generated OTP, timestamp of OTP generation, and user's email. You might name it email_verification.On User Registration: During user registration or when the user asks for a magic link/OTP:Generate a random secret key for the user using a cryptographically secure random number generator. Store this in the email_verification table along with the user's email.Generate the OTP using TOTP methodology and the user's secret key. Store the OTP and the generation time in the email_verification table.Send the OTP to the user's email as part of a magic link or a separate code.On User Verification: When the user clicks on the magic link or enters the OTP:Fetch the OTP and timestamp from the email_verification table for that user's email.If the timestamp is too old (say, more than 10 minutes), reject the verification.If the user clicked a magic link, compare the OTP in the magic link with the OTP from the database. You're correct in assuming that an attacker could potentially exploit the vulnerability of a hardcoded salt, but it's important to understand how and why this could happen.A salt is a random value that is generated for each instance of encryption, and it's usually concatenated with the password (or any other data you're encrypting) before the encryption process. This is particularly effective in preventing pre-computed dictionary attacks, commonly known as rainbow table attacks.A rainbow table attack works by pre-computing the hashes of all possible plaintexts and then storing them. An attacker can then simply look up the hash to get the plaintext. These are effective against systems where the same hash function is used across all records.Salting defends against this because it adds a unique value to each record, which means that pre-computed hashes are no longer effective. In this case, the attacker would need a unique rainbow table for each salt, which is computationally expensive and thus impractical.If you hardcode a salt, then you effectively have a system where the same salt is used across all records. This means an attacker only needs to compute a rainbow table once, which drastically reduces the complexity of an attack.Now, considering your case, where you're not storing the encrypted values anywhere, an attacker would have to intercept your encrypted tokens during transmission. This could happen through various methods, such as packet sniffing, man-in-the-middle attacks, or by gaining access to the email account where the tokens are sent.If the attacker has the encrypted token and the salt (which is hardcoded, and so could be found out by inspecting your system or through other means), then they could attempt a brute force attack to figure out the original payload, or use rainbow tables if the hashing function is known and the salt is the same across all tokens.The advantage of a time-limited token is that even if an attacker manages to intercept and decrypt a token, it will be useless after the expiration time, which adds an additional level of security. This reduces the time window in which an attacker can exploit a stolen token.As for an encryption method that uses a shared secret key and doesn't bother with a salt, you might want to look at symmetric encryption methods, such as AES. AES encryption is very strong and widely used. However, it still requires a key, which should be kept secure and definitely not hardcoded into your system.In summary, while it's true that your method is less susceptible to typical rainbow table attacks, it's still vulnerable to other forms of attacks, particularly if the attacker manages to gain access to your encryption key or your hardcoded salt. Adding unique, per-token salts and keeping your secret key secure will significantly improve the security of your system.

A Time-Based One-Time Password (TOTP) system, like the one we've discussed, indeed adds a significant layer of security.To clarify, in a TOTP system, the one-time password is generated from a shared secret and the current timestamp. The server and the client both generate the TOTP independently and then the client sends its version to the server for verification. If the server's generated TOTP matches the client's TOTP, then the client is authenticated.A key aspect of this is that the shared secret must be securely stored and protected against unauthorized access. In our case, the shared secret is stored in the database and associated with a particular verification event. If an attacker were to gain access to the database and the shared secret, they could theoretically generate the TOTP if the TOTP hasn't expired yet. However, once the TOTP expires, it's of no use to an attacker.So, the primary vulnerability of the TOTP system is the secure storage of the shared secret and the secure communication of the TOTP to the client (e.g., via email or some other means). If the database were to be compromised and the shared secret was stolen, an attacker could potentially generate the TOTP, but again, this is only useful if they are able to do this before the TOTP expires.Overall, implementing a TOTP system, as we've discussed, will provide a robust level of security for your application, particularly if you ensure secure storage of shared secrets and implement a short expiration time for the TOTP. The lack of a salt in the TOTP system is not a significant issue, as each TOTP is unique to a particular timestamp and shared secret, essentially performing a similar function as a salt in password hashing.

Key rotation is indeed a common practice in cryptography to mitigate the risk of key exposure. However, the effectiveness of key rotation in preventing brute-force attacks depends on a few factors:Rotation Frequency: The rotation frequency should be set according to the perceived risk and capability of the attacker. In theory, a higher rotation frequency can make brute-force attacks harder by reducing the time window an attacker has to crack the key. However, too frequent rotation may cause operational issues, and tokens generated with old keys will become invalid unless you maintain a grace period system.Grace Period: As you mentioned, maintaining a grace period during which tokens encrypted with old keys are still accepted can help with operational smoothness during key transitions. However, this also means that the effectiveness of key rotation in preventing brute-force attacks is somewhat reduced, as the time window for cracking the old key is extended.Key Strength: Key rotation can be less effective if the encryption keys are not strong enough to begin with. If your encryption key is weak or guessable, an attacker might be able to crack it before the next rotation.Rotating keys regularly can certainly increase the security of your system, but it's not a silver bullet. You still need to consider other potential vulnerabilities and security measures. For instance, key management and secure storage of keys become more critical in a system with frequent key rotation. If an attacker can access your new keys (e.g., by compromising the system where keys are generated or stored), key rotation won't help much.Another potential vulnerability could be if an attacker is able to intercept the communication between the server and the client (e.g., man-in-the-middle attack). This could reveal not just the encrypted tokens, but also other sensitive information. Therefore, it's important to secure the communication channels as well, e.g., using HTTPS for web traffic.Additionally, secure handling of email communication is critical since the OTP is sent via email. If an attacker can intercept or access the user's email, they can get the OTP. Therefore, secure email practices, such as using secure email servers and encouraging users to use strong email passwords and two-factor authentication, can also be helpful.Lastly, remember that no system is perfectly secure. The goal is to make attacking the system more costly (in terms of time, effort, and resources) than the potential gain from the attack. A layered approach to security, which combines several security measures, can help achieve this goal.

The EDI 204 is a standardized electronic data interchange (EDI) transaction set used in the transportation industry. It is part of the ANSI X12 EDI standard, which defines the format and structure for exchanging business documents electronically.The EDI 204 transaction set, also known as the Motor Carrier Load Tender, is used by shippers or brokers to offer a shipment to a motor carrier. It provides detailed information about the shipment, including pickup and delivery locations, scheduled dates and times, equipment requirements, and other relevant instructions.Here are some of the key data elements typically included in an EDI 204 transaction:Load Identification: A unique identifier assigned to the shipment.Equipment Requirements: Specification of the type and quantity of equipment required for the shipment, such as trailers or containers.Pickup and Delivery Information: Details about the origin and destination locations, including addresses, contact information, and any specific instructions.Dates and Times: Scheduled dates and times for pickup and delivery.Shipment Details: Information about the goods being transported, including weight, quantity, dimensions, and special handling requirements.Special Instructions: Any additional instructions or requirements related to the shipment.By using the EDI 204 transaction, businesses can automate and streamline the process of tendering loads to motor carriers, reducing manual paperwork and improving efficiency in the transportation supply chain.

In the world of mathematics and physics, a non-holonomic system is a system whose state cannot be described fully by a set of generalized coordinates with unconstrained motion. This is in contrast to a holonomic system, where the motion is completely describable by a set of generalized coordinates and is always integrable.Non-holonomic systems are characterized by constraints, specifically non-holonomic constraints, that are velocity-dependent or non-integrable. A classic example of a non-holonomic system is a rolling wheel: the wheel's point of contact with the ground does not slip, which is a constraint involving the velocity of the point of contact.The no-slip condition is a non-holonomic constraint because it cannot be expressed purely in terms of the position of the system, but rather, it also depends on the system's velocity. This non-integrability and dependence on velocity is what differentiates non-holonomic constraints from holonomic ones.Non-holonomic systems present interesting mathematical challenges because they often don't adhere to the principle of least action (or more precisely, they do not admit a Lagrangian description in the conventional sense). This means that the conventional tools of Lagrangian and Hamiltonian mechanics aren't as effective when dealing with these systems, requiring different mathematical treatments, such as non-holonomic mechanics, to properly understand and predict their behavior.A common misconception is that non-holonomic constraints are "non-physical" or "unrealistic". However, this is not true. Many real-world systems (such as cars, bicycles, and wheeled robots) are effectively non-holonomic due to their no-slip conditions. Furthermore, non-holonomic systems can exhibit complex and counterintuitive behaviors that make them interesting subjects of study, both in pure mathematics and in applications like robotics and control theory.It's important to note that while non-holonomic systems don't admit a traditional Lagrangian or Hamiltonian description, there are generalized versions of these formalisms that can handle non-holonomic systems (such as the Vakonomic mechanics). However, these generalized formalisms are more complex and less well-understood than their traditional counterparts.In the context of robotics, non-holonomic systems often require advanced control strategies. A commonly cited paper on this topic is "Nonholonomic Motion Planning: Steering Using Sinusoids" by Richard Murray and S. Shankar Sastry, which proposes a method for steering non-holonomic systems using sinusoidal inputs.

Let's break it down more clearly.In the context of machine learning and the Hugging Face Trainer, an "iteration" refers to a single pass over one batch of data. The number of iterations is equal to the number of batches in your data. In each iteration, the model computes the forward pass, calculates the loss, and then computes the backward pass to get the gradients.When we talk about an "update", we refer to the process where the optimizer uses these gradients to update the model's weights. Normally, this update happens once for every batch of data (i.e., after each iteration).However, if we introduce the concept of "gradient accumulation", the relationship between iterations and updates changes. If gradient_accumulation_steps is set to a number N, then the optimizer will only perform an update every N iterations. In other words, the gradients calculated at each iteration are accumulated (added together) across N iterations, and only then an update is performed using the accumulated gradients.Here's a simplified illustration of what happens when gradient_accumulation_steps=2:Iteration 1: Compute forward pass on Batch 1 -> Compute backward pass to get Gradients 1Iteration 2: Compute forward pass on Batch 2 -> Compute backward pass to get Gradients 2Now perform an update using the sum of Gradients 1 and Gradients 2This process is independent of the type of optimizer used (Adam, SGD, etc.). The reason we might want to do this is primarily for memory considerations. If we want to use a large batch size but don't have enough GPU memory, we can instead use a smaller batch size and set gradient_accumulation_steps to a larger value. The effect is similar to training with a larger batch size because the optimizer is updating the weights based on the same amount of data.In summary:"Iteration step": A single pass over one batch of data, including computing the forward pass, the loss, and the backward pass."Update step": The process of using the gradients to update the model's weights."Gradient Accumulation step": The process of adding together the gradients from multiple iterations before performing an update. The number of iterations per update is determined by gradient_accumulation_steps.

The save_steps argument determines how often checkpoints of the model will be saved during the training process. It's controlled by the save_strategy argument, which can be set to "steps".If save_steps is set to an integer value, then that value is interpreted as the number of update steps to perform between checkpoint saves. So if save_steps is 500, then a checkpoint will be saved every 500 update steps. An update step is when the optimizer uses the gradients to update the model's weights.If save_steps is set to a float in the range [0,1), then it's interpreted as a fraction of the total number of training steps. So, for example, if you have 1000 total training steps and save_steps is set to 0.1, then a checkpoint will be saved every 100 steps (because 1000 * 0.1 = 100).By saving checkpoints periodically, you can resume training from the latest checkpoint if something interrupts your training process. Additionally, you can choose the best checkpoint based on validation performance.

The logging_steps argument in Hugging Face's TrainingArguments indeed specifies how often logging information should be printed to the console.However, it's not just limited to console logging; it affects other forms of logging as well, including any integrated tools like Weights & Biases (wandb), TensorBoard, etc. These logging tools use the same logging_steps parameter to decide how often they should log metrics.For example, if you have Weights & Biases set up and logging_steps is set to 10, then training loss, validation loss, and other metrics will be logged to your Weights & Biases dashboard every 10 steps.It's important to note that logging_steps is defined in terms of update steps, not epoch or batch iteration. If you're using gradient accumulation (with gradient_accumulation_steps > 1), a logging "step" will span multiple batch iterations.Also, remember that excessive logging can slow down your training, so it's usually a good idea to set logging_steps to a reasonable number.

The lr_scheduler_type argument in Hugging Face's TrainingArguments determines what kind of learning rate scheduler will be used during the training process.The learning rate scheduler is a method that adjusts the learning rate during the course of training according to a predefined strategy. Adjusting the learning rate can be helpful in ensuring that the model converges effectively during training.The "constant" scheduler type means that the learning rate remains constant throughout the training process. In other words, the learning rate that you set at the beginning of training with the learning_rate argument will not be changed during the course of training.There are several other types of schedulers available in the transformers library, such as "linear", "cosine", "cosine_with_restarts", "polynomial", and others. Each of these represents a different strategy for adjusting the learning rate during training. For example, a "linear" scheduler would gradually decrease the learning rate from the initial learning rate to 0 throughout the course of training.

Let's try to shape it in a more structured format.Title: The Freedom in "Bad Writing": A Reflection on EntrepreneurshipIntroductionIn her enlightening book, The Right to Write, Julia Cameron criticizes the pressure system ingrained within us from a young age. The doctrine, "If you can't say anything nice - or nicely - don't say anything at all," pushes us towards a type of prose that is lifeless, boring, and often kills the joy of writing. This system that insists on doing things "right" also creates a mindset that restricts creativity in both writing and entrepreneurship.The Paradox of Innovation and ControlThe drive to innovate and make mistakes is as integral to any entrepreneurial process as the seemingly dull part of coordination. These two sides form the axis of a startup's journey, and balancing them is a task unique to each entrepreneur. Yet, the pressure to conform, to follow a well-trodden path to success, often hinders the creative process. Much like a writer fearing to pen "bad" words, an entrepreneur may fear stepping off the beaten path, fearing it might lead to failure.Misconceptions About SuccessIn entrepreneurship, the well-accepted "stones" to success – milestones like acquiring customers, attracting investors, and achieving results – often create a misleading image of the journey. Many successful entrepreneurs will attest that success does not necessarily follow a straight, predictable path. The right "stones" to stumble upon may not be the obvious ones, and the importance of time – often dismissed or underestimated – cannot be overstated.The Power of PermissionDrawing from Cameron's wisdom, the solution to this problem lies in giving ourselves permission. Permission to walk the seemingly impossible path, to write badly, to err as an entrepreneur, is the first pillar in addressing this issue. Real stories aren't made from perfect journeys; they're made from unique, messy, and personal experiences.The Balance Between Creativity and ControlThe second pillar involves recognizing and utilizing the underlying forces that drive us to create. This isn't about advocating for uncontrolled chaos. It is about being strategic, about finding a balance. Abraham Maslow, in Maslow on Management, talks about the creative individual, the one who doesn't attempt to control the outcome. Such individuals are not random; they are merely outside the oppressive system of over-control.Finding Joy in the ProcessThe final pillar is the joy of discovery, the excitement in the journey itself. It involves understanding the joy in the process, and not just in the result. It involves realizing that the success of your venture doesn't have to be a Herculean task requiring years of stress and toil. It could be about finding success in daily achievements, in the process, in the "moments of relaxation" within each day.ConclusionIn the end, the journey of an entrepreneur, much like that of a writer, involves navigating a delicate balance between creativity and control. In both cases, releasing control, allowing ourselves to make mistakes, and finding joy in the process can lead to a more authentic and fulfilling journey. The git rebase and git filter-branch commands both can be used to rewrite the history of a git repository, but they have different purposes and capabilities:git rebase:The git rebase command is primarily used to move or combine a sequence of commits to a new base commit.In interactive mode (-i or --interactive), it can be used to edit previous commit messages, squash commits, or amend the author of a commit.The example provided (git rebase --exec 'git commit --amend --author="Michael Lustig <lustig@knophy.com>" --no-edit -S' --root) uses the --exec flag to execute a command for each commit in a series. This is effectively changing the author of each commit and signing it with GPG. This is less flexible than filter-branch as it doesn't conditionally change the author based on the original author.git filter-branch:The git filter-branch command is more powerful and allows you to rewrite a wider range of aspects of git commits.You can use it to modify the contents of files, directories, commit messages, author names, and more across a range of commits.The example provided uses the --env-filter flag, which allows for more complex scripting to conditionally change the author's name and email based on the original values. However, it does not re-sign the commits with GPG.In summary, while both commands can be used to change the author information, git filter-branch is more powerful and can be used for more complex rewriting tasks. However, it does not automatically re-sign the commits.In your case, since you want to both change the author and re-sign the commits, the git rebase command with the --exec flag is more appropriate. This command is indeed simpler for this specific task.Please note that both commands rewrite history, so they should be used with caution, especially in shared repositories.

論文の初めの部分を確認したところ、以下の情報を得られました：タイトル:
Interpretable bilinear attention network with domain adaptation improves drug-target prediction著者:Peizhen Bai (Department of Computer Science, University of Sheffield, Sheffield, United Kingdom)Filip Miljković (Imaging and Data Analytics, Clinical Pharmacology & Safety Sciences, R&D, AstraZeneca, Gothenburg, Sweden)Bino John (Imaging and Data Analytics, Clinical Pharmacology & Safety Sciences, R&D, AstraZeneca, Waltham, USA)Haiping Lu (Department of Computer Science, University of Sheffield, Sheffield, United Kingdom)概要:
この論文では、薬物とターゲットの相互作用を予測することの重要性が強調されています。最近の深い学習ベースの方法は有望な結果を示していますが、2つの主要な課題があります：(i) 薬物とターゲットの局所的な相互作用をどのように明示的にモデル化し、学習するか、(ii) 異なる分布からの新しい薬物-ターゲットペアの予測の汎用性をどのように確保するか。この研究では、薬物の分子グラフとターゲットのタンパク質配列を用いて予測を行うDrugBAN（deep bilinear attention network）フレームワークを提案しています。このフレームワークは、薬物とターゲットのペアごとの局所的な相互作用を明示的に学習するためのもので、異なる分布のデータに適応する能力も持っています。DrugBANは、学習された相互作用の表現を異なる分布間で整合させ、新しい薬物-ターゲットペアに対する予測の汎用性を向上させるための条件付きドメイン敵対学習を使用しています。また、学習された双線形注意マップを可視化することで、予測結果から解釈可能な洞察を得ることができます。これは概要の一部です。さらに詳しく知りたい情報や特定のセクションについての情報が必要であれば、お知らせください。

"CDAN"は、Conditional Domain Adversarial Networkの略で、異なるドメイン間のデータ分布の違いを軽減するためのドメイン適応技術を指します。この論文のコンテキストにおいて、CDANは、ソースドメインからターゲットドメインへの知識の移転を強化するために使用されます。具体的には、論文ではDrugBANの一部としてCDANを組み込むことで、クロスドメインのDTI（Drug-Target Interaction）予測の性能を向上させることを目指しています。以下は、CDANに関連する論文中のいくつかの引用部分です："If the prediction task is cross-domain, the conditional domain adversarial network (CDAN) module is employed to align learned representations in the source and target domains.""CDAN is a domain adaptation technique to reduce the domain shift between different distributions of data.""We use CDAN to embed joint representation fff and softmax logits ggg for source and target domains into a joint conditional representation via the discriminator, a two-layer fully connected network that minimizes the domain classification error to distinguish the target domain from the source domain.""By minimizing the distribution discrepancy across domains, CDAN can effectively enhance DrugBAN generalization ability and provide more reliable results.""(2018) proposed a novel deep domain adaptation method, CDAN, that combines adversarial networks with multilinear conditioning for transferable representation learning. By introducing classifier prediction information into adversarial learning, CDAN can effectively align data distributions in different domains."これらの引用から、CDANは、異なるドメイン間でのデータ分布の違いを軽減するための効果的な方法として提示されていることがわかります。

Gomez (University of Toronto)Łukasz Kaiser (Google Brain)Illia Polosukhin概要 (Abstract) の内容によれば、この論文は、主要な系列変換モデルが複雑な再帰的または畳み込みニューラルネットワークに基づいていることを指摘しています。これらのモデルはエンコーダとデコーダを含むもので、最も性能の良いモデルは、注意メカニズムを介してエンコーダとデコーダを接続しています。この論文では、再帰や畳み込みを排除し、純粋に注意メカニズムだけに基づく新しいシンプルなネットワークアーキテクチャ、Transformerを提案しています。この概要に基づいて、この論文は、NLP (自然言語処理) のタスクで非常に影響力のあるTransformerアーキテクチャの導入を目的としていると推測されます。Transformerは、再帰的または畳み込みのアプローチを使用せずに、純粋に注意メカニズムを使用して系列データを処理する新しい方法を提供します。論文の詳細や他のセクションの内容についても知りたい場合は、お知らせください。

Self-attentionについての概要として以下を提供いたします。Self-attentionの概要Self-attention、またはintra-attentionとは、シーケンスの異なる位置間の関係を考慮して、そのシーケンスの表現を計算するための注意メカニズムです。このメカニズムは、読解、抽象的な要約、テキストの含意、タスクに依存しない文の表現の学習など、さまざまなタスクで成功を収めてきました。Transformerは、シーケンスアライメントされたRNNや畳み込みを使用せずに、入力と出力の表現を計算するために完全にself-attentionに依存する最初の変換モデルです。エンコーダにはself-attentionレイヤーが含まれており、このレイヤーではすべてのキー、値、クエリが同じ場所、具体的にはエンコーダ内の前のレイヤーの出力から来ています。論文からの引用"Self-attention, sometimes called intra-attention is an attention mechanism relating different positions of a single sequence in order to compute a representation of the sequence.""Self-attention has been used successfully in a variety of tasks including reading comprehension, abstractive summarization, textual entailment and learning task-independent sentence representations.""To the best of our knowledge, however, the Transformer is the first transduction model relying entirely on self-attention to compute representations of its input and output without using sequence-aligned RNNs or convolution.""The encoder contains self-attention layers. In a self-attention layer all of the keys, values and queries come from the same place, in this case, the output of the previous layer in the encoder."これらの情報を基に、Self-attentionはTransformerアーキテクチャで非常に重要な役割を果たしており、文やシーケンス内の各トークンが他のトークンとの関係をどのように考慮して新しい表現を生成するかを示しています。

残念ながら、"attention score"に関する具体的な言及を論文から直接抽出することはできませんでした。ただし、この情報はTransformerの基本的な概念としてよく知られています。Attention Scoreの計算は、Query (Q) と Key (K) ベクトルのドット積として行われ、このスコアはその後、Softmax関数を適用して正規化されます。この正規化されたスコアは、各トークンが他のトークンにどれだけの注意を払うべきかの重みとして使用されます。もしご質問や他の情報を求める場合は、お知らせください。

この論文のタイトルは「Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition」で、Kaiming He, Xiangyu Zhang, Shaoqing Ren, および Jian Sun によって書かれています。彼らはMicrosoft Research所属の研究者のようです。概要によれば、深いニューラルネットワークの訓練は難しいという問題に対して、残差学習フレームワークを提案しています。このフレームワークでは、層を参照なしの関数を学習するのではなく、層の入力を参照にして残差関数を学習する形で明示的に再定式化しています。結果として、これらの残差ネットワークは最適化しやすく、深さを増やすことで精度が向上することが示されています。特に、ImageNetデータセットでの評価では、最大152層の深さを持つ残差ネットワークが評価されています。このネットワークはVGGネットよりも8層深いですが、複雑さは低いです。この残差ネットワークのアンサンブルは、ImageNetのテストセットで3.57%のエラー率を達成しました。この結果は、ILSVRC 2015の分類タスクで1位を獲得しました。この情報から、この論文は深いニューラルネットワークの訓練を容易にするための新しいフレームワーク、特に「残差ネットワーク」に関するものであり、その実験的な結果と評価が述べられていることがわかります。

In Unity 2D, there are two different collision detection modes: Discrete and Continuous. Each mode has different trade-offs in terms of accuracy and performance.Discrete Collision Detection: Discrete collision detection is the default mode in Unity 2D. It works by checking for collisions between objects at discrete time intervals, based on the physics simulation steps. This mode is efficient and suitable for most games, but it can sometimes miss collisions if objects are moving too fast, or if the objects are very small.Continuous Collision Detection: Continuous collision detection is a more accurate mode that works by checking for collisions continuously throughout the frame, instead of at discrete time intervals. This mode is more computationally expensive than discrete collision detection, but it is necessary for fast-moving objects or objects that are small relative to the simulation grid size.To choose a collision detection mode for your game objects, you can set the Collision Detection property of the Rigidbody2D component. By default, the Collision Detection property is set to Discrete, but you can change it to Continuous if you need more accurate collision detection.In general, you should use Discrete collision detection unless you have a specific need for Continuous collision detection, such as when dealing with very fast-moving objects or objects that are small relative to the simulation grid size. Continuous collision detection can significantly impact performance, so you should use it only when necessary.I hope this helps!

Update() and FixedUpdate() are two different methods in Unity that are used to update the state and behavior of game objects during runtime.The main differences between Update() and FixedUpdate() are:Execution rate: Update() is called every frame update, which means it can be called multiple times per frame depending on the frame rate of the game. On the other hand, FixedUpdate() is called at a fixed time interval, typically every physics update, which is usually less frequent than frame updates.Time step: Update() uses the time since the last frame update as the time step, which can vary depending on the frame rate of the game. FixedUpdate(), on the other hand, uses a fixed time step that is controlled by the physics settings in Unity, making it more suitable for physics-related calculations and rigid body interactions.Consistency: Update() may not be called at a consistent rate, as it depends on the frame rate of the game, which can vary on different platforms or under different performance conditions. FixedUpdate(), on the other hand, is guaranteed to be called at a fixed time interval, making it more consistent for physics calculations that require precise timing.Physics interactions: FixedUpdate() is typically used for physics-related calculations and rigid body interactions, as it is called at a fixed time step that aligns with the physics engine's update rate. Update() is typically used for general game logic and other non-physics-related calculations.In summary, Update() is called every frame and is suitable for general game logic, while FixedUpdate() is called at a fixed time interval and is suitable for physics-related calculations and rigid body interactions. It's important to choose the appropriate method based on the specific requirements of your game and the type of calculations you need to perform.

This method is used for handling physics calculations and updating the position, velocity, and other physics properties of the game objects. It is called at a fixed time interval because the physics engine needs to update at a fixed rate to maintain the stability of the simulation.In summary, Update() is used for non-physics related updates and FixedUpdate() is used for physics-related updates.

The FindObjectOfType method can be useful in certain situations, but it's generally not considered the best approach for finding specific objects in your scene.FindObjectOfType searches the entire scene hierarchy for an object of a given type and returns the first match it finds. While it can be convenient for quickly accessing a specific object, it has some drawbacks:Performance: FindObjectOfType can be slower compared to other methods of finding objects, especially if used frequently or in large scenes, as it needs to iterate through all the objects in the scene.Dependency on object order: FindObjectOfType returns the first match it finds, so if you have multiple objects of the same type in the scene, the result may not be consistent if the order changes.Limited flexibility: FindObjectOfType only finds objects based on their type, so if you have multiple objects of the same type but different functionality or states, it may not give you the desired object.Instead of relying heavily on FindObjectOfType, it's generally better to use other approaches for managing and accessing objects, such as:Assigning references: Manually assign references to specific objects in your scripts, either through the Inspector or by dynamically assigning them during runtime.Using singleton pattern: Create a singleton script that manages access to specific objects, allowing you to retrieve them easily from anywhere in your code.Event-driven communication: Use events or delegates to allow objects to communicate with each other without needing direct references.These approaches provide better control and flexibility in managing objects and can help avoid some of the drawbacks associated with FindObjectOfType.

Certainly! The singleton pattern is a design pattern that allows you to have a single instance of a class throughout your program. It ensures that there is only one instance of the class and provides a global point of access to it.Here's a step-by-step explanation of the singleton pattern:Create a class that you want to make a singleton. This class should have a private constructor to prevent external instantiation.Declare a private static variable of the same type as the class. This variable will hold the single instance of the class.Create a public static property or method that allows other parts of the code to access the single instance. This property or method will be used to retrieve the instance.Inside the property or method, check if the instance variable is null. If it is, create a new instance of the class and assign it to the instance variable. If it is not null, return the existing instance.Optionally, you can make the singleton instance persistent between scene changes by using DontDestroyOnLoad() on the game object that holds the singleton instance.By following these steps, you ensure that there is only one instance of the class throughout your program, and you can access it from anywhere using the static property or method.The singleton pattern is useful when you want to have a single, globally accessible instance of a class that manages a specific aspect of your program, such as a game manager, an input manager, or a resource manager. It provides a convenient and efficient way to access and use that instance without having to pass references around or search for the instance in your code.

Yes, the singleton pattern is typically implemented as a separate script that is attached to a specific GameObject in your scene. The singleton script itself does not have a visual representation or functionality tied to a specific GameObject, but it serves as a central point of access for the singleton instance.You can create a separate script file for your singleton class and attach it to an empty GameObject in your scene. This empty GameObject acts as a container for the singleton instance and allows you to easily access the singleton from other scripts in your project.By attaching the singleton script to a GameObject, you can take advantage of Unity's lifecycle events such as Awake, Start, and OnDestroy to initialize and clean up the singleton instance as needed.Remember to ensure that the GameObject with the singleton script is present in the scene at all times when you need access to the singleton instance. If the GameObject is destroyed, the singleton instance will be lost, and a new instance will be created when the script is attached to a new GameObject.

If you have a unique gameObject in the scene with a specific tag, using GameObject.FindWithTag can be a viable approach. It can simplify the process of locating the gameObject without relying on FindObjectOfType or singleton patterns. However, there are a few considerations to keep in mind:Performance: Using GameObject.FindWithTag can be slower than having a direct reference to the gameObject. It performs a search through all the gameObjects in the scene with the specified tag, which can impact performance if you have a large number of gameObjects.Tag uniqueness: Ensure that the tag you assign to the gameObject is unique in the scene. If multiple gameObjects share the same tag, GameObject.FindWithTag will return the first gameObject it encounters with that tag, which may not be the intended gameObject.Maintenance: If you change the tag of the gameObject, you'll need to update the code that uses GameObject.FindWithTag accordingly. This can introduce potential issues if you forget to update all the relevant code.Code readability and debugging: Using explicit references or a dedicated manager script can make your code more readable and easier to debug. It provides a clear indication of which gameObject you are accessing and avoids any potential confusion or conflicts that can arise from using tags.In general, it's best to use direct references or a dedicated manager script whenever possible, as it provides better performance, reduces the chance of errors, and improves code readability. However, if you have a small number of unique gameObjects and you ensure tag uniqueness, using GameObject.FindWithTag can be a practical solution.

The threshold for what constitutes a "large number" of gameObjects can vary depending on factors such as the hardware capabilities of the target platform and the complexity of your scene. However, as a rough guideline, once you start having hundreds or thousands of gameObjects in your scene, you may begin to experience performance issues when using methods like GameObject.FindWithTag.Unity's performance is influenced by several factors, including the number of gameObjects in the scene, the complexity of their components and scripts, the frequency of updates and physics calculations, and the capabilities of the target device. As the number of gameObjects increases, the time required for Unity to search and iterate through them also increases, which can lead to performance degradation.To optimize performance when dealing with a large number of gameObjects, it's recommended to use techniques like object pooling, spatial partitioning, and culling to reduce the number of active gameObjects and minimize unnecessary computations.In summary, the threshold for a "large number" of gameObjects may vary, but as a general guideline, when you start having hundreds or thousands of gameObjects, it's advisable to consider performance optimizations and alternative approaches to GameObject.FindWithTag.

Object pooling is a technique used in game development to efficiently manage and reuse gameObjects. Instead of constantly creating and destroying gameObjects, object pooling involves creating a pool of pre-instantiated gameObjects at the start of the game or level and reusing them as needed.Here's a general overview of how object pooling works:Initialization: During game startup or level loading, a pool of gameObjects is created and instantiated. These gameObjects are typically disabled and stored in a list or data structure.Object Request: When a gameObject is needed in the game, instead of instantiating a new one, an inactive gameObject from the pool is retrieved.Object Activation: The retrieved gameObject is enabled and positioned as required in the game world. It can be customized further with specific properties or components if needed.Object Deactivation: When the gameObject is no longer needed or becomes inactive, it is returned to the pool. It is disabled and reset to its default state so that it can be reused later.By reusing gameObjects instead of creating and destroying them frequently, object pooling reduces the overhead associated with memory allocation and garbage collection. It helps improve performance by minimizing the time spent on instantiation and destruction, especially when dealing with a large number of gameObjects or frequent spawning/destruction of objects.Object pooling is commonly used for managing bullets, particle effects, enemies, and other frequently created/destroyed gameObjects. In programming, the keyword static is used to define members (fields, methods, properties) that belong to the class itself rather than instances of the class. Here are some key points about static members:Static fields: A static field is shared among all instances of a class. There is only one instance of the field regardless of how many instances of the class are created. Static fields are accessed using the class name, followed by the field name (e.g., ClassName.FieldName).Static methods: A static method belongs to the class and can be invoked without creating an instance of the class. Static methods cannot access non-static fields or call non-static methods directly.Static properties: A static property allows you to get or set a value that is associated with the class itself, rather than a specific instance of the class.Static constructor: A static constructor is used to initialize the static members of a class. It is executed only once when the class is accessed for the first time.By marking a member as static, you indicate that it is not tied to a specific instance of the class and can be accessed independently. This is useful when you want to share data or functionality across multiple instances or when you need to access a member without instantiating the class.

Na classificação de texto, precisão e recall são duas métricas importantes que nos ajudam a entender o desempenho do nosso modelo.Precisão: A precisão é a proporção de previsões positivas que foram corretamente classificadas. Em outras palavras, é o número de verdadeiros positivos (ou seja, os itens corretamente identificados como pertencentes à classe positiva) dividido pela soma dos verdadeiros positivos e dos falsos positivos (ou seja, os itens erroneamente identificados como pertencentes à classe positiva). Uma alta precisão significa que, quando o modelo prevê que um exemplo é positivo, ele geralmente está correto.Recall (revocação): O recall é a proporção de exemplos positivos reais que foram corretamente identificados. Em outras palavras, é o número de verdadeiros positivos dividido pela soma dos verdadeiros positivos e dos falsos negativos (ou seja, os itens erroneamente identificados como pertencentes à classe negativa). Um alto recall significa que o modelo identifica corretamente a maioria dos exemplos positivos.Ambas as métricas são importantes e devem ser consideradas em conjunto. Por exemplo, um modelo pode ter alta precisão, mas baixo recall se for muito conservador e apenas fizer previsões positivas quando estiver absolutamente certo. Por outro lado, um modelo pode ter alto recall mas baixa precisão se fizer muitas previsões positivas, incluindo muitas que estão erradas. A métrica F1, que é a média harmônica da precisão e do recall, é frequentemente usada para combinar as duas métricas em um único número.

Claro, posso fornecer exemplos hipotéticos para ilustrar as situações.Alta precisão, baixo recallVamos supor que temos um sistema de filtragem de emails para identificar spam. O modelo foi treinado para ser extremamente cauteloso ao classificar um email como spam (porque, digamos, não queremos que emails importantes sejam erroneamente classificados como spam e acabem na pasta de spam).Dos 1000 emails que recebe, o modelo classifica apenas 10 como spam, e todos os 10 são realmente spam. Portanto, a precisão é de 100% (todos os emails classificados como spam são realmente spam). No entanto, na realidade, havia 100 emails de spam na caixa de entrada. Então, o modelo só identificou 10 dos 100 emails de spam verdadeiros. Portanto, o recall é de 10% (só identificou 10% dos emails de spam verdadeiros).Nesse caso, temos alta precisão (o modelo raramente erra quando diz que um email é spam), mas baixo recall (o modelo perde a maioria dos emails de spam).Baixa precisão, alto recallVamos considerar o mesmo cenário de filtragem de emails. Desta vez, o modelo foi treinado para ser extremamente agressivo ao marcar um email como spam.Dos 1000 emails que recebe, o modelo marca 500 como spam. Todos os 100 emails de spam reais foram identificados e marcados como spam, mas também foram marcados 400 emails que não eram spam. Então, temos 100 verdadeiros positivos e 400 falsos positivos. A precisão, portanto, é de 20% (apenas 20% dos emails marcados como spam são realmente spam).No entanto, o modelo conseguiu identificar todos os 100 emails de spam que estavam na caixa de entrada. Portanto, o recall é de 100% (ele identificou todos os emails de spam verdadeiros).Nesse caso, temos baixa precisão (o modelo faz muitas falsas previsões positivas) e alto recall (o modelo identifica todos os exemplos positivos).

Claro, vamos ver como essas métricas são calculadas usando as fórmulas.Alta precisão, baixo recallO modelo classificou 10 emails como spam, e todos os 10 eram realmente spam. Portanto, temos:Verdadeiros Positivos (TP) = 10Falsos Positivos (FP) = 0 (nenhum email foi erroneamente classificado como spam)A precisão é calculada como TP / (TP + FP), então neste caso é 10 / (10 + 0) = 1, ou 100%.No entanto, havia 100 emails de spam na caixa de entrada, e o modelo só identificou 10 deles. Portanto, temos:Verdadeiros Positivos (TP) = 10Falsos Negativos (FN) = 90 (90 emails de spam não foram identificados)O recall é calculado como TP / (TP + FN), então neste caso é 10 / (10 + 90) = 0.1, ou 10%.Baixa precisão, alto recallO modelo classificou 500 emails como spam, mas apenas 100 deles eram realmente spam. Portanto, temos:Verdadeiros Positivos (TP) = 100Falsos Positivos (FP) = 400 (400 emails foram erroneamente classificados como spam)A precisão é calculada como TP / (TP + FP), então neste caso é 100 / (100 + 400) = 0.2, ou 20%.No entanto, todos os 100 emails de spam foram identificados pelo modelo. Portanto, temos:Verdadeiros Positivos (TP) = 100Falsos Negativos (FN) = 0 (nenhum email de spam foi deixado de identificar)O recall é calculado como TP / (TP + FN), então neste caso é 100 / (100 + 0) = 1, ou 100%.

"On Intelligence" is a book by Jeff Hawkins, the creator of the Palm Pilot and Treo smartphone, with contributions from Sandra Blakeslee. It's a book about brain theory and artificial intelligence. Hawkins proposes a theory called Hierarchical Temporal Memory (HTM), which is based on the idea that the neocortex works on a principle of hierarchical predictive modeling.According to the theory, the neocortex, which is the part of the brain responsible for perception, imagination, thought, and decision making, is a memory-prediction system that works by storing and recalling sequences of patterns. In this view, intelligence is not so much about response times or computational power, but about prediction based on pattern recognition.The hierarchical aspect of the model refers to how the brain processes information. Lower levels of the hierarchy process basic sensory input, such as lines and edges in the visual field. This data is then passed up to higher levels of the hierarchy, which integrate the information to recognize more complex forms, such as objects and concepts. The temporal aspect of the model refers to how the brain anticipates what will come next, based on past experiences.As for counterarguments against Hawkins' model, there are several:Lack of experimental evidence: Hawkins' theory is largely based on observations and thought experiments rather than empirical scientific data. While it's an interesting and potentially useful model, it lacks the kind of rigorous testing and support from experimental data that other cognitive theories have.Underestimation of brain complexity: Some critics argue that the model oversimplifies the complexity of the brain. For instance, it assumes uniformity across different regions of the neocortex, which some researchers argue is not the case. Some parts of the brain, such as the hippocampus, have different structures and may play unique roles in cognition that aren't accounted for by the HTM theory.Inability to account for all cognitive functions: Critics have pointed out that the HTM theory doesn't account for all aspects of cognition. For example, it doesn't explain how emotions influence thought processes, or how the brain makes decisions when faced with conflicting information.Lack of specificity: While the HTM theory provides a general framework for how the brain might process information, it lacks specificity in many areas. For example, it doesn't provide a detailed explanation of how individual neurons contribute to the overall functioning of the brain.While these criticisms highlight areas where the theory may be lacking, they don't necessarily invalidate it. The HTM theory has been influential in the field of artificial intelligence and has inspired many researchers to explore similar approaches. It's an ongoing area of research and debate.

Several researchers have explored similar approaches to the Hierarchical Temporal Memory (HTM) theory. These include:Tai Sing Lee and David Mumford: They proposed a theory of hierarchical cortical computation based on Bayesian belief propagation. While their model is mostly consistent with the HTM theory, the latter adds details about handling invariant representations in the visual cortex​1​.Stephen Grossberg: Grossberg and his team researched LAMINART and similar neural networks. These models aim to explain the infrastructure of the cortex and the behavior of neurons in a temporal framework to explain neurophysiological and psychophysical data. However, these networks are currently too complex for realistic application​1​.Tomaso Poggio: Poggio's work is also related to HTM, including an approach for modeling the ventral stream of the visual cortex known as HMAX. The similarities of HTM to various AI ideas are described in the December 2005 issue of the Artificial Intelligence journal​1​.Kunihiko Fukushima: Professor Fukushima proposed the Neocognitron, a hierarchical multilayered neural network, in 1987. This model is one of the first deep learning neural network models, sharing similarities with the hierarchical structure of HTM​1​.Please note that while these researchers have explored similar themes or structures, their specific models, hypotheses, and findings may differ in significant ways from the HTM theory as presented by Jeff Hawkins.

Kunihiko Fukushima's Neocognitron is a type of artificial neural network inspired by the hierarchical, multilayered structure of the visual cortex in animals. It was one of the earliest models of what we now call "deep learning". The Neocognitron was designed to recognize visual patterns and was a significant influence on later convolutional neural networks, a popular model in modern machine learning.The Neocognitron is made up of multiple layers of "cells", each of which has a specific function:S-cells (Simple cells): These cells perform local feature extraction. They are designed to respond to specific patterns, such as lines at particular orientations. The S-cells in higher layers respond to more complex patterns, which are combinations of the features detected by the S-cells in lower layers.C-cells (Complex cells): These cells perform a pooling operation, which makes the network invariant to shifts and distortions of the input pattern. If a pattern is recognized by an S-cell, then a C-cell connected to that S-cell will still respond even if the pattern is shifted or distorted.In the Neocognitron, the S- and C-cells are arranged in alternating layers. The S-cells in the first layer respond to simple features in the input, and the C-cells in the next layer pool these responses. The S-cells in the second layer then respond to more complex features made up of combinations of the simple features detected by the first layer, and so on.One of the most notable features of the Neocognitron is that it can recognize patterns regardless of their position or size in the input field. This characteristic, known as "shift and distortion invariance", is a key feature of many modern deep learning systems.While the Neocognitron was a groundbreaking development, it's worth noting that it lacks some of the features of modern deep learning systems. For example, the original Neocognitron didn't use backpropagation, a common method for training neural networks. Despite these differences, the Neocognitron laid much of the groundwork for later developments in deep learning.

Чтобы составить таблицу возможных значений N с их вероятностями, нам нужно рассмотреть все возможные сценарии игры.Пусть W обозначает победу одной команды, а L — победу другой команды. Используя эти обозначения, составим таблицу:N=1: W, L
P(N=1) = P(W) + P(L) = 0.5 + 0.5 = 1N=2: WW, LL
